And it’s, I guess, administrative and business offices for full time employees at the camp, which is called these days, it’s called the Washington, Washington Family Camp. It’s named after the gentleman in Montana who purchased the property in 1991 and then donated a few years later to the Young Life Organization. So that building’s still there and that was kind of the epicenter of Rajneeshpuram.

Up the road from there is another important building that’s in a little bit of disrepair, but it’s still standing. It’s called Magdalena. It was the cafeteria and commercial bakery. And they were pumping out 600 loaves a day that were being sold. What they didn’t use, they were selling to stores like Madras and Portland or whatever. So they called it Maggie’s place and so Maggie’s is still standing. Ma non Sheila’s house or the place she lived, I didn’t get to see this, but I’m told that it still exists and it’s been converted into guest quarters for like when high-end guests come to visit the Washington family ranch. So that’s still standing. The Bhagwan’s house evidently burnt in a wildfire in 1997. What else is existing? The Meditation Center, which was like I think ten thousand square feet, it was huge. But it was built when they had the first International Rajanish festival there. But now it’s just this huge sports center with basketball courts and all of this other stuff. So, and it’s because it’s a kids’ camp in the summer. So they built a water park into the side of one of the cliffs for the kids. There’s all these buildings the kids can live in, but the A-frames.

There’s still a lot of housing still left, but some of those A-frames were purchased by a couple who live in Antelope, Oregon. They are a fifth generation ranching family, and they bought the old antelope market that when the Raj Nishis took over Antelope and took over the city council, they took the town center, the social meeting hub, the antelope market and turned it into the Zorba the Buddha market and had a kitchen. They were selling wine there as well. So she and her husband bought ten of those old A-frames and they’re right next to the market and they did the roof a little bit but you can stay in them overnight now. You can rent them and stay there for like 45 bucks a night and they’re being used by long distance bike riders, people that go out into the desert to do rock hunting.

But it’s a dark sky sanctuary city, Antelope is. So people that come with all their equipment to look at stars, to take pictures of plants and stuff like that. So those A-frames are booked all the time. at 45 and a little higher if you want sheets. I slept in a sleeping bag. But on the inside of the A-frame, it was the original woodworking that was done by the Roshanishi carpenters. And in Antelope Market, which looks great, she and the couple that refurbished it did a great job.

They still have the original wine racks that the Rajanishis built. So whoever the carpenters who made these were really good because there’s not a scratch on these. They are so lacquered and hard, there’s no scratches. It looks brand new. The mark, the cuttings for the bottle heads to fit in were exquisitely done. And so they’re using them to sell wine now, just like the Rajanishis did using the same racks. So that’s where the A that’s where some of the A-frames are. But a lot of that stuff is still up there.

SV

And, like what does it feel like? You know, for anyone who doesn’t know the story, I mean, there was a lot of crazy stuff that went on, including murder attempts, Sheila poisoned the salad bar and was it in the Dalles?

MA

In the Dalles, yeah, in the Dalles. There was a lot of stuff. There were a few state officials who came in that claimed that they had been attempted when they were visiting there. Attempt to assassinate Bhagwan’s personal physician. There was a lot of internal power play stuff going on with Sheila, who was more I think more than just the right hand person. She was really kind of

in control for a large period of the existence of Rajneesh Brahm. They got upset with a public land use dispute. So the building where the records were kept was mysteriously burnt to the ground. It was arson. so yeah there were a lot of crimes that were committed for sure. Sheila did time in a federal pit prison in California for being convicted of what she was accused of.

And the Bhagwan was found guilty on immigration charges and said, You have to leave the country, you can’t come back. So yeah, there was a lot of wrongdoing that went on. But in a wild, wild country, the documentary really, you know, does a good job of focusing on that. The people I talk to, and folks out there should know that there are still thousands of followers of what is now called Osho, around the world. They are very private for obvious reasons, they’re not really up to talking to the media or public people too much. So I had to go through a lot of back channels and back doors, friends of friends making references to talk to. But the people that I talked to said, yeah, there was some stuff going on. But our day-to-day lives

That wasn’t part of our day to day lives. That was power plays up at the top. We were doing farming, we were doing agriculture, we were building things with our hands, and we were having a great time. And we thought it was dynamite. And so it’s kind of this wistful thought, sort of like this vineyard story. There’s this wistful thought about what could have been if, you know, things had been kept under control, if Sheila hadn’t organized the things she did. There was this thought that this could have been something really beautiful. And so that was, you know, the kind of the image. And from talking to people, the Wild Wild Country documentary’s been out long enough that some of the original hubbub has kind of died off. But there was a sense that it didn’t capture everything and it couldn’t possibly. It captured the stuff that was the most sensationalistic, is what people would say to me when I would talk to them. It captured the most sensationalistic aspects. But then there was this other side of day-to-day life within Rajneesh Pram that wasn’t captured as well. And for obvious reasons, it’s not a sexy thing compared to the stuff that was in the documentaries. So they said.

In terms of things like the vineyard and the wine culture, yeah, they said that’s an important part of the story too.

SV

Yeah, I mean I I know with Wild Wild Country there has been some criticism of some of the other things that hasn’t captured, like the allegations of child abuse and some of those issues. And I know that you’ve spoken to some of those like abuse survivors who have encouraged you to report on the day to day.

You’ve talked to so many people. Like, what is the consensus of or is there a consensus of like what went on? Like, do people think it was a cult? I know some are still following Osho, as you mentioned.

MA

I think that technically the textbook definition of a cult is, sure, the original Rajanish Brahm with one leader claiming some kind of divine influence and sure, call it a cult. I think what exists now is more decentralized. They’re not following an individual person so much it didn’t seem like it seemed like

From talking to the people I interviewed, they were taking the lessons they learned while they lived there, and they were continuing to use those philosophies in their day-to-day lives. So they were taking the good things and replicating those now. And one guy that I talked to is running a meditation center in Seattle. Another person I talked to is running a global cranial therapy company.

But I’ll tell you what, not a single individual I talked to that lived there. And I asked everybody I talked to, I said, it is a story about a vineyard and the wine culture at Rajnish Pram, is that trivial in comparison to some of these other things that happened there? Should I write the story? Is it just too flippant to write a story about this given what happened? And every single person said, Absolutely, you should tell the story.

One of the people I talked to said, you can’t tell the total story if you only tell the bad side. And you have to tell the good side as well. And that gives people a total picture. And then let them figure out how they feel about it. But show both sides. And so this vineyard and wine culture story is about that other side of day-to-day life that was totally removed from the politics and Sheila and wiretapping and you know, trying to poison people at a salad bar and all that stuff.

SV

My mom would not eat at salad bars throughout my entire childhood, and I’m pretty sure that that’s why.

MA

I think that’s a great philosophy, even if this hadn’t happened. I watch how people act at salad bars and I wouldn’t touch a salad bar with a ten-foot pole. But the thing with Sheila probably definitely caused more than a few people. I think if I recall stories in the mid-80s, there were restaurants in Oregon that had salad bars that discontinued them for a while, if not forever after that incident because people were so paranoid of it. But

a part of the story is to me it’s personal. It’s an Oregon story. It’s whether it’s negative or positive, it’s it’s an important part of the history of the state as to what happened because you had

Two to three thousand people descend upon a small town. They annexed a neighboring town to get around difficulties with public land use issues because basically they wanted to build a town, and people in Antelope were like, okay, we were okay if it was a small farm, but a town with up to ten thousand people, no way. So they just had to take over the city council of Antelope to get the things they wanted to do done. That’s an important part of Oregon’s land use history.

10,000 friends of Oregon got involved in this. So this was a pretty big deal. And it was a huge deal. And like my father-in-law worked for the Central Oregon Electrical Cooperative in that area. So I was always hearing stories about what was going on with Rosh Nishprom and Antelope. And so I think for a lot of Oregonians, it’s a personal story, people of a certain age. Like I was in college when this was happening.

I have a vivid memory of it and you know, a lot of people still draw lessons from what happened to this day with land use planning and stuff. And religious tolerance.

SV

Yeah, and I think it’s you know, to show the good side, I feel like so often when you bring up conversations about cults or like these religious communities that, you know, when things go awry, so often people are like, How would you end up in that situation? Like, why’d you make that choice? And I feel in general, like most people are smart, so

There’s gotta be some kind of draw to be involved in that sort of community in that situation.

MA

Yeah, absolutely. I think one of the biggest misconceptions people that I talk to, even if they’ve seen the Wild Wild Country documentary, I think there’s this perception that the Rajneshis were coming to follow a cult guru and that they were brainwashed, that they were like old nineteen late 1960s hippies looking for a new thing to follow, and that they had come to Oregon to give up all their worldly possessions. And it’s like nothing could be further from the truth.

So I’ve got this study. The University of Oregon went out and surveyed the folks living at Rajanishpuram and they found out that 81% of the people there came from families with professional and white-collar backgrounds, middle to upper middle class. and they were highly educated. 64% of the people living in Rajanishpuram had graduated from college.

I think for the state of Oregon, the average was like 17%. So this was a fairly educated group. And like that group, 26% had advanced degrees. So this was a smart, you would think, rationally thinking group that had decided capitalism wasn’t doing them much good. Maybe the world was going to check in a handbasket and this would be a good place to create the next step.

So my favorite quote came from one of the people I interviewed, Jason Siever, the founder of Wine Spies in California, who lived there with his parents when he was like 13 to 17 years old. and his quote was: My parents arrived with multiple master’s degrees, and I saw all kinds of PhDs that were driving tractors and medical doctors that were working on the road group. So

They accomplished in the first year with a lot of people that didn’t necessarily know how to build a road or to build a house within a year, they the list of things that they constructed in terms of infrastructure, in terms of irrigation, roads, damming up rivers to eliminate erosion problems, creating lakes, planting trees, planting crops. I mean, in the first year, they just transformed this little dry sagebrush covered. Horribly over-farmed, depleted area, and made something out of it where something would grow. And they did it within a year. And Chintan, I think, told me that when the first group of people arrived, that there were only like 60 to 80 of them. Mostly, you know, 24 to 34 years old, in good shape, smart.

Some of them had expertise in some areas, most didn’t. and they did that within a year. So I do tip my cap to the get it done, the stick-to-itiveness of that town and that group of people. So that’s one thing that kind of resonated with me. And when I saw those buildings still standing, still in great shape, in a climate that does not lend itself to buildings surviving through frost and cold and all that stuff.

Yeah, there was still a lot there. and it was impressive what they accomplished. So yeah, it was as if they were not late sixties hippies just looking to hang out and meditate. There was a lot of meditation, but you know, there was more to it than what people think. I you know ,

SV

If you were to sum up what their philosophy was that they were following like b the Bhagwan Osho what would it be? I see I often come across like Osho quotes on Instagram or something and I’m like, well that’s pretty deep, you know, and it seems like there’s a lot of things I I have these moments where I’m like, I kind of resonate with that and then I’m like, wait, wild, wild country.

Yeah, what were these people, you know, what were they following? What were they believing?

MA

I think it’s just the longer I did this, and so this is like five plus years of doing this on and off, working on this story, I think it boils down to being nice to each other and taking care of the earth. So the sustainability part of it was a big deal to what they were trying to do. They had seen a world in the mid-80s coming out of the 70s, oil problems in the Mideast, depletion, conflict. And so they kind of saw this as an opportunity to start over. And so it was kind of I. It sounds simplistic, but it’s like be nice to each other and do some good and you know work on the ground, make something. There was a lot of I kept hearing that phrase, it’s like do something. if somebody was standing around evidently someone would walk up to somebody and go, hey, do something.

And you know, there wasn’t a lot of idle time because they had a lot of stuff to build. So I think that’s kind of what it boiled down to me. And you know.

Every person I talked to was so nice and forthcoming. You know, once I got to I mean once I got through the three layers of stuff that they’ve you know, there’s private Facebook groups, private Reddit groups, and all this. Once you get past that and they kind of trust what you’re doing, everybody was very forthright, very, very gentle and kind. You know, even Ma Anan Sheela. She lived the brief interaction I had with her. It was like talking to somebody’s grandmother. I mean she just had to keep it in your head thinking, my god, I’m talking to this woman. She tried to poison people and assassinate people and she just seems like someone’s grandmother, so you know, kind and had a little bit of a sense of humor based on the little five brief conversations and a few emails I had with her. So yeah I was, they were just really nice to talk to. And they’ve put Raj Nish Pram, the day-to-day existence, a lot of that stuff they put behind them. I mean, people are getting older. A lot of people that I tried to get in touch with that were major players within the wine community there had died within the last couple of years.

So you know, their day-to-day memory of what was going on in Rajadish Prahmus kind of drifted. But I’ll tell you this, and I think Chintan’s quote in the article about it, is even people that lived there for four years that I talked to, some of them were like, We had no idea that we had a vineyard. We had no idea that there was a vineyard out there. And part of that is is it’s you know, it’s a nice walk, it’s a long drive to get from

Downtown Rajneeshpuram where the strip mall was, Devertith, to get out to where the dairy barn was and all the agricultural stuff was going on, you know, that wasn’t it wasn’t an easy trek. So I could see now, having been there, I could see why people would be totally oblivious to the vineyard part of it. However, the wine culture part of it was kicking. They had a wine store where they had Wednesday night tastings. Every tasting was themed. People were paying. I mean, it operated like a bottle shop in New York City. You had to come in and pay for your tasting. One week it would be Rhone wines. One week I saw that it was like Spanish wines. And so there’d be Wednesday night tastings. You could buy bottles of wine. They had numerous Oregon Liquor Control Commission licenses, package licenses. They were pouring in their various restaurants. They had all sorts of food themes.

You could eat pizza, there was French food, Indian food, there was a wide variety of foods you could eat. There was wine everywhere being poured by the bottle and by the glass, and they were selling bottles out of the deli. And in Antelope, they were selling bottles out of the old antelope market. So there was a really thriving wine culture there. A lot of mostly Australian wines. A lot of the people that were involved in agriculture on the truck farm and out in the vineyard area, had worked in Australia. They knew what dry farming was. And so there was a lot of Australian wines on the shelf. But I’ve seen photographs of the old Delhi wine store, and I could pick out on the shelves vintage ports, what looked like vermouth, some Spanish wines, some sparkling wine that would have probably had to have been champagne. It was a pretty nice little selection of wines they had to choose from.

SV

You’ve mentioned to me that like the Rajneeshees came within like, I think you said like an eyelash of disrupting the Oregon like wine industry, especially like the Willamette Valley, which was kind of, you know, getting a foothold at the time. Tell us a little bit more about that.

MA

Yeah, so they had plans. So nine acres was already planted and they were definitely gonna make commercial wine, no doubt about it. Chintan said we were gonna make wine commercially. And so it was the summer of eighty five and he had like was trying to get the money together to buy a bottling line.

Or something like that. And the money had gone. The money had run out because of all the legal difficulties, Sheila, all of that. Everything was starting to wind down. And so that was it. That was the end of it. They never got to make that first vintage of wine. But if they’d have been allowed to go, they would have put onto the market in 85 and into 86, you know, something around 1100 cases of wine. And nobody really in Oregon was making that much wine at the time.

And they would have gone out onto the market with a lot of competitive advantages. They were getting the fruit for free. The grapes were free. The labor was free. The money that was being brought into what would have been the winery was money coming in from donations from the outside world and from people that were giving up some of their income to live in Raj Nishprom. And so they could have pretty much named their price.

I’m guessing based on talking to Chintan, Chintan knew what he was doing. I think the wines would have been good. They were smart enough not to try to make Pinot Noir as a red wine, because they knew at 1,400 feet above sea level, and with the climate they had, frost would be an issue, ripening would be an issue. So they were gonna do a lot of early ripening, early picking stuff. So they were gonna make a rose of pinot noir, and then they were gonna make dry white wines or white wines.

Can’t say they were all gonna be dry, but they were gonna make white wines with the Riesling Gewerts from here and Chardonnay, and that is what they were gonna do. And as they brought in income, the plan was to expand the vineyard to 30 acres. And Jintan said there were a lot of places on the property where they could have expanded and planted other vineyards. So the plan was if things went well, they would expand. And so part of that expansion was building a small winery facility.

in Rajneeshpuram and under one roof they planned to have a kind of a tasting room. And it sounds like a modern tasting room. What they had planned was actually a little ahead of its time because it was like this complete table to farm experience. Under one roof they were gonna have wine tastings and sell wines. They were going sell eggs, dairy, bread

baked goods they were making herbal products, you know, like cosmetics, lavender, herbal things, and they were gonna sell all that under one roof to draw in tourism. And, you know, I would have loved to have seen what that would have turned into, all the politics and Sheila stuff aside, if that hadn’t happened, that would have been to me a really interesting place to go visit.

I have no doubt that given the charismatic individuals they would have sent out into the marketplace to get their wines placed in restaurants and bottle shops, I think they would have done okay. I think they would have done well.

SV

And are there any wineries or vineyards in the area now?

MA

Yep. not immediately close to Antelope and where Raj Nish Pram is, but if you go from Antelope about another eighteen to twenty miles or so back towards a town called Madras, Madras, Terrebonne, Prineville, Bend, and Redmond.

There are vineyards in those areas. In fact, they are working on making an application to the federal government for an AVA called Deschutes, a Deschutes AVA that’ll have a lot of those wineries in it. But for the most part, a lot of them are doing Minnesota hybrid grapes that can tolerate the winters. So you’ve got a lot of marquette and things like that. a little bit of Vita Spinifra stuff going on out there, but

Some of those hybrid wines that I’ve tasted, some of them have been really good. So I you know, I think there’s a future down there for this stuff. but

You know, they weren’t doing those hybrids weren’t available really to the Rashnishis. Chinten said that he knew he studied Washington and the area around the Walla Walla Valley and Yakima and he realized the climate was pretty similar. S roughly the same amount of rainfall in a year, like twelve to twenty inches, you know, and average temperatures were similar. So he drove up there to see about buying cuttings and he was told

We would love to sell you cuttings, but you can’t just take back across the state border and plant them. They have to go through quarantine. There’s all this paperwork. And he said, Okay, all right, fine. And he said, Forget it. And then the next year in spring of eighty-two, he drove up to the Willamette Valley, knowing that he had to buy cuttings from in the state, and bought all of the cuttings that were used to plant the vineyard from a nursery in the Willamette Valley. Now, in nineteen eighty-two there were only two, maybe three.

Potential nurseries that were selling cuttings. Chintan can’t remember who he bought them from. And the late Dick Erath, who had a nursery, is a very famous Oregon winemaker, who’s now dead, so I can’t talk to him about this. Chintan said, I bought it from a nursery, and the odds are really good that he bought his cuttings from Dick Erath’s nursery, which was an important historical piece of the Willamette Valley wine industry. I would have paid money.

Chintan was this good-looking young guy with a beard and flowing hair, and he would have been wearing all the red and stuff and the beaded necklace and everything. And then here’s gruff Dickie Rath with a sense of humor. I would have loved to have seen the conversation between those two when he told them I want to buy cuttings to plant them in the middle of you know the central Oregon high desert. It would have been good to hear. But we can’t prove anything, we don’t know, but it’s definitely from the Willamette Valley and from the nursery for those cuttings.

SV

Well, and now it sounds like the the wine history of Rajneesh Param that I had never heard of before is out there for public consumption and knowledge, so

MA

Yeah, I mean that was the thing that really got me about this story was I watched Wild Wild Country and then I went and was doing some reading and saw the reference to the vines which got this whole thing going. But so I went back and watched it again and I had to make sure that there were no wine references because I thought if there’s a vineyard reference in here or a wine reference or if they show the video I mean that kind of takes a little of the steam out of the story. But the thing that kept getting me was that every corner I turned, nobody had ever heard of this vineyard. Oregon winemakers, I mean, other than maybe the person who sold them the cuttings, but every winemaker I talked to had no idea that this was going on. None. Period. They were flabbergasted. And even people that lived there didn’t know the vineyard was going on for the most part. So yeah, I thought that was just a mind boggling part of the story. It was how did this lay it sit there all these years and nobody knew anything about it? So

SV

Well, thank you for bringing it to us. I know I’ve been absolutely fascinated by the story of the Rajneehis overall, but especially the wine culture now. So I’m glad that we’ve been able to dive into it and get to know what actually happened on that side of the street.

MA

Yeah.

MA

And I’ll leave people with one last thing, which is if anybody’s interested in the story of Rajnishpuram and what happened, in the town of Antelope, there is an old three story white clapboard building that used to be a union hall that was built in 1898. The building used to house this little kind of informal Rajneeshpuram museum. Wynne McCormick recently purchased it, who’s like co-founder of Mother Jones magazine, editor in chief at New Republic. During the eighties, he covered Rajneesh Param for his Oregon magazine. I think he did some writing for us at Oregon. But he purchased that building. And I think in the spring of 2027 or sometime soon, it is now the Wynn McCormick Rajnish Param Museum. And he’s putting all of his papers and all of his stuff in there. And this was the building where the Rajnish Times newspaper was also printed. So there’s a lot of Rajneesh Param stuff in there, memorabilia, written records, photographs. I think a lot of things people have never seen before. So when that opens, I think that’s going to be a great way to study what happened there.

SV

Amazing. So go visit Antelope.

MA

Go visit Antelope, stay in an A frame.

SV

Well, thank you Michael. It’s been an absolute pleasure.

MA

All right, thank you.

title: The Most Bizarre Tale in the History of Oregon Wine
summary:
If you think the Rajneeshees were a bunch of counter-culture types who renounced all worldly pursuits, think again.

The post The Most Bizarre Tale in the History of Oregon Wine appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
I thought I knew all of Oregon’s best wine stories. I missed the one about the Indian guru who nearly launched a winery before his utopian community collapsed.

Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh, a.k.a. Osho, came to the United States in January 1981, ostensibly seeking medical treatment for back pain. His move may have also been due to tax issues with the Indian government and the need to find more space for his growing number of followers.

Six months later, Bhagwan’s personal secretary, Ma Anand Sheela, orchestrated the purchase of 64,229 acres of remote, highdesert land in Oregon’s Wasco County.

As any good guru does, Bhagwan had amassed a large group of devotees. They worked long hours to transform the area locals called the Big Muddy Ranch into an incorporated city named Rajneeshpuram. Eventually, they would also annex the neighboring town of Antelope—a move that did not sit well with its 40 residents

Thanks to attempted political assassinations, arson, a bioterror attack, immigration-fraud charges, and other legal troubles, the Rajneeshpuram experiment came to a screeching halt at the end of 1985 amid allegations of child abuse at the commune.

Cut to 2021, when I finally got around to binge-watching Wild, Wild Country, the Netflix docuseries about Rajneeshpuram. It inspired me to pick up a copy of historian Frances FitzGerald’s book, Cities on a Hill: A Journey Through Contemporary American Cultures. In the chapter on Rajneeshpuram, FitzGerald wrote, “Since July of 1981, the Rajneeshee had—they said—cleared 3,000 acres of land and planted them with winter wheat, sunflowers, vegetables, vines, and fruit trees.”

Vines? I’ve been covering Oregon wine for decades. How did I not know about this? I had a lot of questions.

The Search for Answers

My investigation began with an artist named Rashid Maxwell, known in his Rajneesh days as Swami Deva Rashid. Rashid worked in agriculture at Rajneeshpuram, so I hoped he could shed some light on these mysterious vines. He said he didn’t spend much time in the vineyard and pointed me toward Swami Veet Chintan, who was responsible for planting Rajneeshpuram’s grapevines. Chintan was happy to share all the vineyard details through a series of phone calls and emails from his home in Slovenia.

Chintan brought a good deal of expertise to Rajneeshpuram when he arrived in July 1981. He earned a master’s degree in agriculture in Switzerland, studying viticulture and winemaking. At Rajneeshpuram, he helped establish a dairy farm named Rabiya. He traveled to Washington State to purchase cuttings for the commune’s vineyard, but came home empty-handed due to the red tape involved with transporting vine cuttings across state lines.

So Chintan headed to the Willamette Valley and successfully sourced cuttings from a nursery. I suspected it was Dick Erath’s famed nursery, but he said he wasn’t sure. In the fall of 1982, Chintan helped plant 12,500 Chardonnay, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir, and table grape vines in Rajneeshpuram’s nineacre vineyard.

“I remember that we planted the vines with six feet between rows and four feet between vines along one row,” Chintan said. Backed by rock-strewn slopes and dramatic cliff walls, the southward-facing vineyard sat at an elevation of 1,420 to 1,480 feet.

Did the vineyard have a name? Chintan said he didn’t know of any, but added that, “I’m sure someone in one of our departments had a name in mind.”

The vineyard’s location was remote, even by Rajneeshpuram standards. “Not many people knew what we were doing out there,” Chintan said.

He worked closely with Rajneeshpuram’s farm coordinator, an Australian named Swami Anand Neehar. “It was a team effort, where I would help with pruning the vines and checking the irrigation, but I was mostly consulting with Neehar and supervising others,” Chintan said.

A sophisticated Israeli drip irrigation system supplied water to the vineyard. This system predated Argyle Winery’s pioneering irrigation efforts in the Willamette Valley, which started in 1988.

By 1983, grapes began appearing on the vines that Chintan and Neehar had shepherded from infancy. Those first grapes made their way to Magdalena, the commune’s 10,000-square-foot cafeteria and bakery.

Disaster struck the next winter when temperatures in the vineyard dropped to 30 degrees below zero. Chintan supervised the cutting back of the vines, which basically meant starting over.

After a small harvest in 1984, fruit production ramped up in 1985. The wine writer James Conaway toured Rajneeshpuram with Neehar that summer. Conaway described the visit for an article in the academic journal The Hedgehog Review: “He is taking me on a tour in his pickup, past the dairy barn, fields redolent of irrigation sewage, and a vineyard expected to produce 14 tons of grapes that Bhagwan intended to turn into a distinguished wine.”

That “distinguished wine” wasn’t going to be limited to on-commune consumption. “We absolutely planned to make wine commercially,” Chintan told me. Neehar boldly predicted they would make 16,000 bottles of wine in 1986.

The name “Wasco White” was jokingly suggested for one of the wines, a nod to the county where Rajneeshpuram was located. One vineyard worker told a reporter for The Rajneesh Times, Rajneeshpuram’s paper of record, that “Chateau Rajneesh” had a nice ring to it.

Swami Prartho Subhan, an attorney and avid wine buff, brought wine to the commune from Baltimore. At one tasting Subhan hosted, he poured a 1970 Beaulieu Vineyards Georges de Latour Private Reserve Cabernet Sauvignon for his friends in Rajneeshpuram. It did not surprise me at all to learn that Subhan had tasted wine back home in Maryland with another attorney, Robert M. Parker, Jr.

Wine tastings were held every Wednesday evening inside a deli called Zorba the Buddha Rajneesh. The deli was also a bottle shop with an Australian Shiraz-heavy inventory. The Rajneesh Times declared in a January 1985 article that “Rajneeshpuram is wine country,” noting that sales at the deli and the Zorba the Buddha Restaurant and Lounge were “brisk.”

With a population of around 2,000 people, having several Oregon Liquor Control Commission licenses to sell and pour wine, beer, and spirits was impressive. The Rajneeshees were hardly teetotalers. Subhan, who now runs a meditation center in Seattle, told me, “There’s so much more to Rajneeshpuram than what you saw in Wild, Wild Country.”

Work Hard, Shop Harder

If you think the Rajneeshees were a bunch of counter-culture types who renounced all worldly pursuits, think again. “We’re not hippies,” Sheela told a reporter for The Oregonian newspaper in January 1983. “Bhagwan teaches us the Rolls-Royce style. We’re a bunch of capitalists.”

The Rajneeshes coveted the lifestyle perks they had enjoyed before arriving in rural Oregon, and Devarteerth Mall was where they could indulge their material desires. Like any good 1980s mall, Devarteerth offered several places to eat, a clothing boutique, a beauty parlor, and a stereo store. At the Omar Khayyam Lounge and Cardroom, guests could quaff alcoholic beverages while boogieing to “It’s Raining Men” by The Weather Girls.

My favorite discovery, however, was that The Rajneesh Times had an excellent weekly wine column. The columnist was Swami Shanti Prabhu, also known as Tim McCarthy, who died in 2021. His brother, Dano McCarthy, told me that Prabhu likely picked up his expertise while working in sales for a wine distributor. One week, Prabhu would recommend an obscure sparkling wine from Côtes du Rhône, and the next week he would be off in the Jura region or recommending a Grignolino from Piedmont. Few wine columns in early-1980s American newspapers covered this much ground.

There was clearly a lot of interest in wine in Rajneeshpuram, but by the time Chintan was ready to start making some in 1985, there was no money left for equipment. “After all the work that we did to keep that vineyard going, it was incredibly disappointing,” Chintan said.

It is hard to resist daydreaming about what might have been if Rajneeshpuram had survived. Free labor, vineyard expertise, and good equipment would have been quite the competitive advantage in the Oregon wine market.

Fortunately, we have a document that gives us a glimpse of that future: the “City of Rajneeshpuram Comprehensive Plan.” Rajneeshpuram’s City Council described it as the “official guide for its future development.” The plan describes building a small winery to “produce Eastern Oregon rosé and white wines.” The Rajneeshees also hoped to expand their vineyard to 30 acres. After assessing the local climate, the document predicts growing more than three to four tons of grapes per acre and producing more than 2,000 bottles per acre. That would have been a lot of wine by 1980s Oregon standards.

Caller on the Line

For me, the most surreal part of this story occurred during Thanksgiving dinner with my family in 2021. That’s when Sheela called me. Sheela was Bhagwan’s right hand, the often-strident spokesperson whom Oregonians frequently saw in segments about the commune on local news.

I had left a phone message and sent an email to the nursing-home business Sheela operated in Switzerland. I never in a million years thought that she would respond.

Sheela was polite and charming on the phone, but she didn’t remember much about Rajneeshpuram’s wine culture, and only vaguely remembered people planting grapes. She claimed that she had her mind on “more important things” at the time. I asked Sheela if she had any favorite wines, Oregon or otherwise. She said that she was surrounded by good Swiss wines where she lived in the village of Maisprach. It was hard to reconcile the sweet voice on the other end of the phone with Sheela’s criminal convictions in the United States. But it did get me thinking: Given all of the terrible things that occurred at Rajneeshpuram, was I wrong to write an article about something so frivolous as the commune’s wine?

I asked Dickon Kent, who lived in Rajneeshpuram as a young boy, if I should proceed. Kent had been instrumental in connecting me with people who had lived in Rajneeshpuram.

“Why not?” Kent replied. “I think it’s good to celebrate the good and the bad that happened. And that’s coming from somebody who was just featured in a documentary about the child abuse at Rajneeshpuram. I think it’s the big piece that a lot of people seem to miss—there is light and dark to everything, and if we’re not willing to acknowledge them both, we’re missing half the story.”

The other half of the story is the stuff of daydreams, even if they went unfulfilled. A Rajneeshee winery would have benefited from low overhead and, thanks to its commercial baked goods and produce operations, a distribution network that ran all the way to Portland. Who knows, Chateau Rajneesh might have gone on to become an Oregon cult classic.
